title: Treasure Baskets
strapline: A low basket of real, beautiful things — and a baby free to choose what their hands and mouth find out today.
intent: Offer sitting babies rich sensory information from real materials — wood, metal, wicker, shell, fabric — that plastic cannot give.
Strengthen reaching, grasping, transferring and releasing as hands work on objects of different weights and shapes.
Support deep, self-chosen concentration: the baby decides what to pick up, mouth, bang and drop, and for how long.
Build shared attention and early communication as treasures are held up, shown and offered to a trusted adult.
Root exploration in emotional safety — a key person close, calm and unhurried is part of the provision.
Lay the earliest foundations of comparing and finding out: heavy and light, cool and warm, loud and silent.
implementation: Sit the baby steadily (cushions behind a new sitter) with the basket within easy reach, and settle yourself close by on the floor.
Be present but not directing: attentive face, relaxed body, no 'look at this one!' — the baby leads, you anchor.
Respond warmly when the baby shows you a treasure — meet their gaze, name it softly ('the spoon — it's cold'), and give it back.
Watch for schemas: the banger, the mouther, the dropper, the poster — and let each baby research in their own way.
Refresh the basket regularly and follow fascinations — more chains for the dangler, more lids for the poster.
Check every object daily: size (no choke hazards), splinters, loose parts; wash mouthables after each session.
End when the baby ends — turning away, fussing or crawling off is the session's natural close, not a schedule.
key_questions: You've gone back to the wooden ring three times — what does it do that the others don't?
Is the metal spoon cold on your cheek? Your face tells me it is!
What will you find at the bottom of the basket?
That was a big bang — shall we listen — can you make it again?
Which treasure is coming to show me?
Where has the pinecone gone — is it hiding under the muslin?

impact.text: Babies sit at the basket reaching in, grasping treasures, passing them hand to hand and straight to the mouth to find out more.
Babies explore natural and household materials with every sense — mouthing the wooden ring, stroking the pastry brush along a bare arm, sniffing the lemon.
A baby works on one object deeply — banging the tin, posting the chain into the cup, dropping the ball again and again to watch what happens.
Babies glance back to their key person mid-exploration, take in the warm face, and return to the basket — exploring from a safe base.
A baby holds the whisk up towards their key person, pointing and vocalising — 'look at this!' — sharing the discovery.
When the key person softly names a treasure, the baby turns to the voice, studies their face, and answers in babble — a real conversation over a shell.
When the basket is lifted away, a baby reaches, bounces and calls for it — asking for more in their own unmistakable way.

enhancements: A metal-only basket for a session — spoons, whisk, tea strainer, small tins — everything cold, shiny and loud.
Natural treasures gathered on the pram walk: large pinecones, a smooth stone, a chunk of bark (checked and sized for safety).
Textile treasures: velvet ribbon, a loofah, sheepskin offcut, crocheted ball — a basket for stroking and scrunching.
Things that nest and hide: fabric bags with a treasure inside, a tin with a lid, a muslin to peep under.
Scent tied in gently — a lavender bag, a whole lemon, a cinnamon stick (supervised) — for noses as well as hands.
Pairs of the same object so two babies alongside each other can research the same treasure without a tussle.
A photo for the family of today's favourite treasure — 'she chose the honey dipper every time' — inviting treasure-gathering from home.

playing_exploring: The baby chooses freely from the basket, following their own fascination with no right way to play.
Every sense is put to work — objects are mouthed, banged, stroked, sniffed and stared at.
active_learning: Babies persist at self-set problems — getting the chain into the tin, reaching the treasure at the bottom.
Concentration runs long and deep when no one interrupts; the same object is revisited across days.
creating_thinking: Babies try their own experiments — will the ring bang like the spoon did, what happens if I drop it over there?
They begin predicting what objects do, and show surprise and delight when the world answers back.
